*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(-1+2t)\,i+(1+t)\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=-\,i+\,j$ and $b=i+2\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(-i+\,j)+t[(i+2\,j)-(-i+j)] \\  & =(-i+\,j)+t(2\,i+\,j) \\  & =(-1+2t)\,i+(1+t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=-1+2t,\,y=1+t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\sqrt[3]{x}\,i+{y}^{6}\,j \\  & =\sqrt[3]{-1+2t}\,i+(1+t)^{6}\,j \\  & =\sqrt[3]{2t-1}\,i+(t+1)^{6}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1+2t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)j \\  & =2\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\sqrt[3]{2t-1}\,i+(t+1)^{6}\,j)\cdot (2\,i+j) \\  & =\sqrt[3]{2t-1}\cdot 2+(t+1)^{6}\cdot 1 \\  & =2\sqrt[3]{2t-1}+(t+1)^{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2\sqrt[3]{2t-1}+(t+1)^{6}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-479e7987-52fe-5f2a-ac6f-211f33047ce8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,j$ and $C$ is the line segment traversed from the point $A(-1,-2)$ to the point $B(3,4)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(-1+4t)\,i+(-2+6t)\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=-i-2\,j$ and $b=3\,i+4\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(-i-2\,j)+t[(3\,i+4\,j)-(-i-2\,j)] \\  & =(-i-2\,j)+t(4\,i+6\,j) \\  & =(-1+4t)\,i+(-2+6t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=-1+4t,\,y=-2+6t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(-1+4t+2-6t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(-1+4t-2+6t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(1-2t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(10t-3)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1+4t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2+6t)j \\  & =4\,i+6\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(1-2t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(10t-3)\,j)\cdot (4\,i+6\,j) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(1-2t)\cdot 4+\operatorname{sin}⁡(10t-3)\cdot 6 \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡(1-2t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(10t-3).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4\operatorname{cos}⁡(1-2t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(10t-3)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cad5fa44-4c82-5eaf-a5e3-0f5d2ccc6820"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id traversed from the point $A(2,1)$ to the point $B(3,3).$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=2\,i+j$ and $b=3\,i+3\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(2\,i+j)+t[(3\,i+3\,j)-(2\,i+j)] \\  & =(2\,i+j)+t(i+2j) \\  & =(t+2)\,i+(2t+1)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t+2\,y=2t+1.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =4(x+y)\,i-3x\,j \\  & =4(3t+3)\,i-(3t+6)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+2)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+1)j \\  & =i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(4(3t+3)\,i-(3t+6)\,j)\cdot (i+2\,j) \\  & =4(3t+3)\cdot 1-(3t+6)\cdot 2 \\  & =6t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6t\,dt \\  & =3{t}^{2}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =3-0 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f6500bd7-63b7-5ff0-8a52-5b1a962545e2"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id *Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(-2+3t)\,i+(1-2t)\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=-2\,i+j$ and $b=i-j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(-2\,i+j)+t[(i-j)-(-2\,i+j)] \\  & =(-2\,i+j)+t(3\,i-2\,j) \\  & =(-2+3t)\,i+(1-2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=-2+3t,\,y=1-2t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(x+y)^{2}\,i+{e}^{x-y}\,j \\  & =(-2+3t+1-2t)^{2}\,i+{e}^{-2+3t-(1-2t)}\,j \\  & =(t-1)^{2}\,i+{e}^{5t-3}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2+3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t)j \\  & =3\,i-2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((t-1)^{2}\,i+{e}^{5t-2}\,j)\cdot (3\,i-2\,j) \\  & =(t-1)^{2}\cdot 3+{e}^{5t-3}\cdot (-2) \\  & =3(t-1)^{2}-2{e}^{5t-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3(t-1)^{2}-2{e}^{5t-3}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1f913e6a-566c-57ec-ae58-510ebea86214"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id \begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(-i-j)+t[-2\,i-(-i-j)] \\  & =(-i-j)+t(-i+j) \\  & =(-1-t)\,i+(t-1)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=-1-t,\,y=t-1.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(y-x)^{2}\,i-xy\,j \\  & =(t-1+t+1)^{2}\,i-(t-1)(-1-t)\,j \\  & =4{t}^{2}\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1-t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)j \\  & =-i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(4{t}^{2}\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j)\cdot (-i+j) \\  & =4{t}^{2}\cdot (-1)+({t}^{2}-1)\cdot 1 \\  & =-3{t}^{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-3{t}^{2}-1\,dt \\  & =(-{t}^{3}-t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(-1-1)-(-0-0) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-22aada0e-297e-544e-8d81-c05bfd8f1190"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={e}^{t}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{t})\,j \\  & ={e}^{t}\,i+t\,j.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{t}\,i+t\,j)\cdot (i+{e}^{t}\,j) \\  & ={e}^{t}+t{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}\,j)\cdot (i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}}\,j) \\  & =t\cdot 1+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}\cdot \frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}} \\  & =2t.\end{aligned}

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2)\,i+t\,j,\,1\le t\le {e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2,\,y=t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\sqrt{y}\,i+{e}^{x}\,j \\  & =\sqrt{t}\,i+{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2}\,j \\  & =\sqrt{t}\,i+t{e}^{2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\sqrt{t}\,i+t{e}^{2}\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{t}\,i+j) \\  & =\sqrt{t}\cdot \frac{1}{t}+t{e}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}+{e}^{2}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}+{e}^{2}t)\,dt.\end{aligned}

{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. This is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =t\,i+{e}^{2t}\,j,\,0\le t\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y={e}^{2t}.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={x}^{2}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j \\  & ={t}^{2}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{2t}\,j \\  & ={t}^{2}\,i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2t})j \\  & =i+2{e}^{2t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({t}^{2}\,i+2t\,j)\cdot (i+2{e}^{2t}\,j) \\  & ={t}^{2}\cdot 1+2t\cdot 2{e}^{2t} \\  & ={t}^{2}+4t{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}+4t{e}^{2t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t(t+4{e}^{2t})\,dt.\end{aligned}

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)={e}^{x}\,i+{e}^{-2y}\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(0,1)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={e}^{x}\,i+{e}^{-2y}\,j \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c6e03b21-80ec-5be8-9b81-321307ca2b39"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=2x\,i+5y\,j$ and $C$ is the the arc of the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $2$ and $4$ respectively, traversed anticlockwise from $A(2,0)$ to $B(0,4).$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to find the parametrization of an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $2$ and $4$ respectively. It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2x\,i+5y\,j \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+20\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+20\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+20\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =72\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =72{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ce1ed3f7-4051-55ee-8dd8-c7e73caeb3e4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+9{sin}^{2}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

where $F(x,y)=-x\,i+y\,j$ and $C$ is a circle of radius $4$ centered at the origin, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction." :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a circle of radius $4$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+y\,j \\  & =-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =16\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =32\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =16\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,dt \\  & =-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t){|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-8+8 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-70d6c2d2-5cd3-5ed9-a60d-0559257216bb"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-70d6c2d2-5cd3-5ed9-a60d-0559257216bb" :answer-field/id #uuid "70d6c2d2-5cd3-5ed9-a60d-0559257216bb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-d8247ec2-f7ab-5814-8d82-ad9c6d067e3e" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d8247ec2-f7ab-5814-8d82-ad9c6d067e3e" "answer-f8b7ad7b-8dd4-56ba-9f6e-701e837c4775" "answer-5d05fea1-c2dc-5ed1-983c-3cd1bdea51ce" "answer-63baee51-af86-53ee-921b-9301ac9943be" "answer-0a2b4e96-c35f-5329-ad67-9ac58f667665"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d8247ec2-f7ab-5814-8d82-ad9c6d067e3e" :answer/id #uuid "d8247ec2-f7ab-5814-8d82-ad9c6d067e3e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f8b7ad7b-8dd4-56ba-9f6e-701e837c4775" :answer/id #uuid "f8b7ad7b-8dd4-56ba-9f6e-701e837c4775" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "16" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5d05fea1-c2dc-5ed1-983c-3cd1bdea51ce" :answer/id #uuid "5d05fea1-c2dc-5ed1-983c-3cd1bdea51ce" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "16\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-63baee51-af86-53ee-921b-9301ac9943be" :answer/id #uuid "63baee51-af86-53ee-921b-9301ac9943be" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "32" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0a2b4e96-c35f-5329-ad67-9ac58f667665" :answer/id #uuid "0a2b4e96-c35f-5329-ad67-9ac58f667665" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "32\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179864 :activity/expected-seconds 1080.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(-1+2t)\,i+(1+t)\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=-\,i+\,j$ and $b=i+2\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(-i+\,j)+t[(i+2\,j)-(-i+j)] \\  & =(-i+\,j)+t(2\,i+\,j) \\  & =(-1+2t)\,i+(1+t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=-1+2t,\,y=1+t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\sqrt[3]{x}\,i+{y}^{6}\,j \\  & =\sqrt[3]{-1+2t}\,i+(1+t)^{6}\,j \\  & =\sqrt[3]{2t-1}\,i+(t+1)^{6}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1+2t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)j \\  & =2\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\sqrt[3]{2t-1}\,i+(t+1)^{6}\,j)\cdot (2\,i+j) \\  & =\sqrt[3]{2t-1}\cdot 2+(t+1)^{6}\cdot 1 \\  & =2\sqrt[3]{2t-1}+(t+1)^{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2\sqrt[3]{2t-1}+(t+1)^{6}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-479e7987-52fe-5f2a-ac6f-211f33047ce8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,j$ and $C$ is the line segment traversed from the point $A(-1,-2)$ to the point $B(3,4)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(-1+4t)\,i+(-2+6t)\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=-i-2\,j$ and $b=3\,i+4\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(-i-2\,j)+t[(3\,i+4\,j)-(-i-2\,j)] \\  & =(-i-2\,j)+t(4\,i+6\,j) \\  & =(-1+4t)\,i+(-2+6t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=-1+4t,\,y=-2+6t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(-1+4t+2-6t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(-1+4t-2+6t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(1-2t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(10t-3)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1+4t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2+6t)j \\  & =4\,i+6\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(1-2t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(10t-3)\,j)\cdot (4\,i+6\,j) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(1-2t)\cdot 4+\operatorname{sin}⁡(10t-3)\cdot 6 \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡(1-2t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(10t-3).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4\operatorname{cos}⁡(1-2t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(10t-3)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cad5fa44-4c82-5eaf-a5e3-0f5d2ccc6820"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=2\,i+j$ and $b=3\,i+3\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(2\,i+j)+t[(3\,i+3\,j)-(2\,i+j)] \\  & =(2\,i+j)+t(i+2j) \\  & =(t+2)\,i+(2t+1)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t+2\,y=2t+1.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =4(x+y)\,i-3x\,j \\  & =4(3t+3)\,i-(3t+6)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+2)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+1)j \\  & =i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(4(3t+3)\,i-(3t+6)\,j)\cdot (i+2\,j) \\  & =4(3t+3)\cdot 1-(3t+6)\cdot 2 \\  & =6t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6t\,dt \\  & =3{t}^{2}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =3-0 \\  & =3\end{aligned}

"question-6205682e-6a34-5394-bdf6-22819f2b4d42" :question/id #uuid "6205682e-6a34-5394-bdf6-22819f2b4d42" :question/math-academy-id "q-125044" :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(x+y)^{2}\,i+{e}^{x-y}\,j$ and $C$ is the line segment traversed from the point $A(-2,1)$ to the point $B(1,-1)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(-2+3t)\,i+(1-2t)\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=-2\,i+j$ and $b=i-j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(-2\,i+j)+t[(i-j)-(-2\,i+j)] \\  & =(-2\,i+j)+t(3\,i-2\,j) \\  & =(-2+3t)\,i+(1-2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=-2+3t,\,y=1-2t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(x+y)^{2}\,i+{e}^{x-y}\,j \\  & =(-2+3t+1-2t)^{2}\,i+{e}^{-2+3t-(1-2t)}\,j \\  & =(t-1)^{2}\,i+{e}^{5t-3}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2+3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t)j \\  & =3\,i-2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((t-1)^{2}\,i+{e}^{5t-2}\,j)\cdot (3\,i-2\,j) \\  & =(t-1)^{2}\cdot 3+{e}^{5t-3}\cdot (-2) \\  & =3(t-1)^{2}-2{e}^{5t-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3(t-1)^{2}-2{e}^{5t-3}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1f913e6a-566c-57ec-ae58-510ebea86214"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=-i-j$ and $b=-2\,i.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(-i-j)+t[-2\,i-(-i-j)] \\  & =(-i-j)+t(-i+j) \\  & =(-1-t)\,i+(t-1)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=-1-t,\,y=t-1.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(y-x)^{2}\,i-xy\,j \\  & =(t-1+t+1)^{2}\,i-(t-1)(-1-t)\,j \\  & =4{t}^{2}\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1-t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)j \\  & =-i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(4{t}^{2}\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j)\cdot (-i+j) \\  & =4{t}^{2}\cdot (-1)+({t}^{2}-1)\cdot 1 \\  & =-3{t}^{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-3{t}^{2}-1\,dt \\  & =(-{t}^{3}-t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(-1-1)-(-0-0) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-22aada0e-297e-544e-8d81-c05bfd8f1190"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-88b1af01-ca8c-54ff-810f-7581fa6aee53" :question/id #uuid "88b1af01-ca8c-54ff-810f-7581fa6aee53" :question/math-academy-id "q-125036" :question/problem "Evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)={e}^{x}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j$ and $C$ is the curve $y={e}^{x}$ traversed from the point $A(0,1)$ to the point $B(2,{e}^{2}).$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Since $y$ is the subject of the equation, a parametrization is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =t\,i+{e}^{t}\,j,\,0\le t\le 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y={e}^{t}.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={e}^{t}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{t})\,j \\  & ={e}^{t}\,i+t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})j \\  & =i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{t}\,i+t\,j)\cdot (i+{e}^{t}\,j) \\  & ={e}^{t}+t{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({e}^{t}+t{e}^{t})\,dt \\  & =t{e}^{t}{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2{e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ce53d1c1-5bca-58e1-b9ee-b33918bcfde9"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=x\,i+y\,j$ and $C$ is the curve $y=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+9}$ traversed from the point $A(0,3)$ to the point $B(4,5).$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Since $y$ is the subject of the equation, a parametrization is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =t\,i+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}\,j,\,0\le t\le 4.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =t\,i+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9})j \\  & =i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}\,j)\cdot (i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}}\,j) \\  & =t\cdot 1+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}\cdot \frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}} \\  & =2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{4}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}2t\,dt \\  & ={t}^{2}{|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =16\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-53f24906-9587-5d21-abdc-d9f2ac613180"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id *Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2)\,i+t\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. This is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2)\,i+t\,j,\,1\le t\le {e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2,\,y=t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\sqrt{y}\,i+{e}^{x}\,j \\  & =\sqrt{t}\,i+{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2}\,j \\  & =\sqrt{t}\,i+t{e}^{2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\sqrt{t}\,i+t{e}^{2}\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{t}\,i+j) \\  & =\sqrt{t}\cdot \frac{1}{t}+t{e}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}+{e}^{2}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}+{e}^{2}t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4c91b1e8-4070-5bcd-8192-983151e5056d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id *Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=t\,i+(2{t}^{2}-1)\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. This is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =t\,i+(2{t}^{2}-1)\,j,\,1\le t\le 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=2{t}^{2}-1.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}-1)j \\  & =i+4t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1)\,j)\cdot (i+4t\,j) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1)\cdot 4t \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{1}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4t\operatorname{sin}⁡(2{t}^{2}-1)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-243882e8-5b20-5cd8-9637-d6f35b444dae"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id *Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=t\,i+{e}^{2t}\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. This is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =t\,i+{e}^{2t}\,j,\,0\le t\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y={e}^{2t}.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={x}^{2}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j \\  & ={t}^{2}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{2t}\,j \\  & ={t}^{2}\,i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2t})j \\  & =i+2{e}^{2t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({t}^{2}\,i+2t\,j)\cdot (i+2{e}^{2t}\,j) \\  & ={t}^{2}\cdot 1+2t\cdot 2{e}^{2t} \\  & ={t}^{2}+4t{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}+4t{e}^{2t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t(t+4{e}^{2t})\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-41f1f87b-e755-58bb-9c62-b95f8a22f0a6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-41f1f87b-e755-58bb-9c62-b95f8a22f0a6" :answer-field/id #uuid "41f1f87b-e755-58bb-9c62-b95f8a22f0a6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-02315312-3684-5faa-a71f-6939225f794e" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e445ee3a-80b3-5bb3-ba14-012400aa2c7c" "answer-da2b15aa-cb0c-58bb-a375-02709c3833e3" "answer-02315312-3684-5faa-a71f-6939225f794e" "answer-775c713e-b491-5879-ae04-90cb3115c486" "answer-d174d4e7-af1d-58cf-bd63-b6b4febdb84a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e445ee3a-80b3-5bb3-ba14-012400aa2c7c" :answer/id #uuid "e445ee3a-80b3-5bb3-ba14-012400aa2c7c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{1}4t(1+{e}^{2t})\,dt" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-da2b15aa-cb0c-58bb-a375-02709c3833e3" :answer/id #uuid "da2b15aa-cb0c-58bb-a375-02709c3833e3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{1}t(t+4)\,dt" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-02315312-3684-5faa-a71f-6939225f794e" :answer/id #uuid "02315312-3684-5faa-a71f-6939225f794e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{1}t(t+4{e}^{2t})\,dt" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-775c713e-b491-5879-ae04-90cb3115c486" :answer/id #uuid "775c713e-b491-5879-ae04-90cb3115c486" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}(1+2{e}^{2t})\,dt" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d174d4e7-af1d-58cf-bd63-b6b4febdb84a" :answer/id #uuid "d174d4e7-af1d-58cf-bd63-b6b4febdb84a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}+2{e}^{2t}\,dt" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180172 :question/problem "![](images/48/4807f92defb4202359a32ca046073cd138db396a0975164e42b96126ac0cc591.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)={e}^{x}\,i+{e}^{-2y}\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(0,1)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={e}^{x}\,i+{e}^{-2y}\,j \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c6e03b21-80ec-5be8-9b81-321307ca2b39"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=2x\,i+5y\,j$ and $C$ is the the arc of the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $2$ and $4$ respectively, traversed anticlockwise from $A(2,0)$ to $B(0,4).$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.$*" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to find the parametrization of an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $2$ and $4$ respectively. It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2x\,i+5y\,j \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+20\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+20\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+20\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =72\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =72{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ce1ed3f7-4051-55ee-8dd8-c7e73caeb3e4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id the arc of a circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point $(0,3)$ to the point $(-3,0).$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+9{sin}^{2}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+9{sin}^{2}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-9\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+27{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =9\operatorname{cos}⁡t(3{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }9\operatorname{cos}⁡t(3{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & =9{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t(3{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & =9{[{sin}^{3}⁡t-\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡t}{2}]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =9[0-(1-\frac{1}{2})] \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a60002fd-79c9-55af-8350-d15ad8aa640e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a60002fd-79c9-55af-8350-d15ad8aa640e" :answer-field/id #uuid "a60002fd-79c9-55af-8350-d15ad8aa640e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-7b6ccc95-f5af-538e-adc2-b6c8fdfcacc8" :answer-field/choices ["answer-08339a10-b80f-5555-8e33-e4cd3d9e86b5" "answer-7b6ccc95-f5af-538e-adc2-b6c8fdfcacc8" "answer-5773a110-68a4-55f1-abfc-418c6517f35e" "answer-02e28cc7-f7f3-51e1-bea0-158eef714f3a" "answer-1263d5b8-2a16-5cf4-bfba-339ea29a3a16"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-08339a10-b80f-5555-8e33-e4cd3d9e86b5" :answer/id #uuid "08339a10-b80f-5555-8e33-e4cd3d9e86b5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{7}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7b6ccc95-f5af-538e-adc2-b6c8fdfcacc8" :answer/id #uuid "7b6ccc95-f5af-538e-adc2-b6c8fdfcacc8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{9}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5773a110-68a4-55f1-abfc-418c6517f35e" :answer/id #uuid "5773a110-68a4-55f1-abfc-418c6517f35e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{9}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-02e28cc7-f7f3-51e1-bea0-158eef714f3a" :answer/id #uuid "02e28cc7-f7f3-51e1-bea0-158eef714f3a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1263d5b8-2a16-5cf4-bfba-339ea29a3a16" :answer/id #uuid "1263d5b8-2a16-5cf4-bfba-339ea29a3a16" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{7}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180015 :question/problem "Evaluate ${∮}_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=y\,i-x\,j$ and $C$ is a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction." :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i-x\,j \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-{sin}^{2}⁡t-{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =-({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-1)\,dt \\  & ={-t|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-2\pi \end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-84019ffa-a424-5feb-9be8-03a303ad719a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

As a result,

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =16\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =32\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =16\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.\end{aligned}

$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=-\,i+\,j$ and $b=i+2\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(-i+\,j)+t[(i+2\,j)-(-i+j)] \\  & =(-i+\,j)+t(2\,i+\,j) \\  & =(-1+2t)\,i+(1+t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\sqrt[3]{x}\,i+{y}^{6}\,j \\  & =\sqrt[3]{-1+2t}\,i+(1+t)^{6}\,j \\  & =\sqrt[3]{2t-1}\,i+(t+1)^{6}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1+2t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)j \\  & =2\,i+j.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\sqrt[3]{2t-1}\,i+(t+1)^{6}\,j)\cdot (2\,i+j) \\  & =\sqrt[3]{2t-1}\cdot 2+(t+1)^{6}\cdot 1 \\  & =2\sqrt[3]{2t-1}+(t+1)^{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(-i-2\,j)+t[(3\,i+4\,j)-(-i-2\,j)] \\  & =(-i-2\,j)+t(4\,i+6\,j) \\  & =(-1+4t)\,i+(-2+6t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=-1+4t,\,y=-2+6t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(-1+4t+2-6t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(-1+4t-2+6t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(1-2t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(10t-3)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1+4t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2+6t)j \\  & =4\,i+6\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(1-2t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(10t-3)\,j)\cdot (4\,i+6\,j) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(1-2t)\cdot 4+\operatorname{sin}⁡(10t-3)\cdot 6 \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡(1-2t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(10t-3).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4\operatorname{cos}⁡(1-2t)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(10t-3)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-f6d2f16c-f6f5-5918-ae9d-9d7f59f7eba9" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-cad5fa44-4c82-5eaf-a5e3-0f5d2ccc6820" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-32efcb37-d58e-5a20-a421-a7a716960b49" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=2\,i+j$ and $b=3\,i+3\,j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(2\,i+j)+t[(3\,i+3\,j)-(2\,i+j)] \\  & =(2\,i+j)+t(i+2j) \\  & =(t+2)\,i+(2t+1)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t+2\,y=2t+1.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =4(x+y)\,i-3x\,j \\  & =4(3t+3)\,i-(3t+6)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+2)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+1)j \\  & =i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(4(3t+3)\,i-(3t+6)\,j)\cdot (i+2\,j) \\  & =4(3t+3)\cdot 1-(3t+6)\cdot 2 \\  & =6t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6t\,dt \\  & =3{t}^{2}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =3-0 \\  & =3\end{aligned}

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=-2\,i+j$ and $b=i-j.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(-2\,i+j)+t[(i-j)-(-2\,i+j)] \\  & =(-2\,i+j)+t(3\,i-2\,j) \\  & =(-2+3t)\,i+(1-2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=-2+3t,\,y=1-2t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(x+y)^{2}\,i+{e}^{x-y}\,j \\  & =(-2+3t+1-2t)^{2}\,i+{e}^{-2+3t-(1-2t)}\,j \\  & =(t-1)^{2}\,i+{e}^{5t-3}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2+3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t)j \\  & =3\,i-2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((t-1)^{2}\,i+{e}^{5t-2}\,j)\cdot (3\,i-2\,j) \\  & =(t-1)^{2}\cdot 3+{e}^{5t-3}\cdot (-2) \\  & =3(t-1)^{2}-2{e}^{5t-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3(t-1)^{2}-2{e}^{5t-3}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-6205682e-6a34-5394-bdf6-22819f2b4d42" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-1f913e6a-566c-57ec-ae58-510ebea86214" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-421f01b5-2cf6-557c-be0b-ca7da3ee40a5" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$a=-i-j$ and $b=-2\,i.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =(-i-j)+t[-2\,i-(-i-j)] \\  & =(-i-j)+t(-i+j) \\  & =(-1-t)\,i+(t-1)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t=1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=-1-t,\,y=t-1.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(y-x)^{2}\,i-xy\,j \\  & =(t-1+t+1)^{2}\,i-(t-1)(-1-t)\,j \\  & =4{t}^{2}\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1-t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)j \\  & =-i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(4{t}^{2}\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j)\cdot (-i+j) \\  & =4{t}^{2}\cdot (-1)+({t}^{2}-1)\cdot 1 \\  & =-3{t}^{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$

:question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Since $y$ is the subject of the equation, a parametrization is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =t\,i+{e}^{t}\,j,\,0\le t\le 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y={e}^{t}.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={e}^{t}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{t})\,j \\  & ={e}^{t}\,i+t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})j \\  & =i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{t}\,i+t\,j)\cdot (i+{e}^{t}\,j) \\  & ={e}^{t}+t{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({e}^{t}+t{e}^{t})\,dt \\  & =t{e}^{t}{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2{e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-88b1af01-ca8c-54ff-810f-7581fa6aee53" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-ce53d1c1-5bca-58e1-b9ee-b33918bcfde9" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Since $y$ is the subject of the equation, a parametrization is given by

$$

$$

$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =t\,i+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9})j \\  & =i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}\,j)\cdot (i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}}\,j) \\  & =t\cdot 1+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}\cdot \frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}} \\  & =2t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{4}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}2t\,dt \\  & ={t}^{2}{|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =16\end{aligned}

["question-7481ae6d-9732-54c0-9a0f-c47726a9f80a" :question/math-academy-id "q-125143"] ["question-7481ae6d-9732-54c0-9a0f-c47726a9f80a" :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=\sqrt{y}\,i+{e}^{x}\,j$ and $C$ is the curve $\operatorname{ln}⁡y=x-2$ traversed from the point $A(2,1)$ to the point $B(4,{e}^{2})?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=(\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2)\,i+t\,j.$*"] ["question-7481ae6d-9732-54c0-9a0f-c47726a9f80a" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. This is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2)\,i+t\,j,\,1\le t\le {e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2,\,y=t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\sqrt{y}\,i+{e}^{x}\,j \\  & =\sqrt{t}\,i+{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2}\,j \\  & =\sqrt{t}\,i+t{e}^{2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\sqrt{t}\,i+t{e}^{2}\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{t}\,i+j) \\  & =\sqrt{t}\cdot \frac{1}{t}+t{e}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}+{e}^{2}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{{e}^{2}}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}+{e}^{2}t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-7481ae6d-9732-54c0-9a0f-c47726a9f80a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-4c91b1e8-4070-5bcd-8192-983151e5056d" :answer-field/id #uuid *Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=t\,i+{e}^{2t}\,j.$*"] ["question-e11373c8-2017-5040-89cd-e12dc0c5ae7b" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. This is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =t\,i+{e}^{2t}\,j,\,0\le t\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y={e}^{2t}.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={x}^{2}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,j \\  & ={t}^{2}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{2t}\,j \\  & ={t}^{2}\,i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2t})j \\  & =i+2{e}^{2t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({t}^{2}\,i+2t\,j)\cdot (i+2{e}^{2t}\,j) \\  & ={t}^{2}\cdot 1+2t\cdot 2{e}^{2t} \\  & ={t}^{2}+4t{e}^{2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}+4t{e}^{2t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t(t+4{e}^{2t})\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e11373c8-2017-5040-89cd-e12dc0c5ae7b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-41f1f87b-e755-58bb-9c62-b95f8a22f0a6" :answer-field/id #uuid Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)={e}^{x}\,i+{e}^{-2y}\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin traversed counterclockwise from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(0,1)?$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.$*"] [17592186180172 :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & ={e}^{x}\,i+{e}^{-2y}\,j \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186180172 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-c6e03b21-80ec-5be8-9b81-321307ca2b39" :answer-field/id #uuid "c6e03b21-80ec-5be8-9b81-321307ca2b39"] Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=2x\,i+5y\,j$ and $C$ is the the arc of the ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $2$ and $4$ respectively, traversed anticlockwise from $A(2,0)$ to $B(0,4).$

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.$*"] ["question-d9322f25-3d78-5fb4-87e7-1e944f82fbf4" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to find the parametrization of an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $2$ and $4$ respectively. It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2x\,i+5y\,j \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+20\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$

$$

Finally, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =72{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt.\end{aligned}

point $(0,3)$ to the point $(-3,0).$"] ["question-17a6c1da-e7e7-5509-a937-e43376741415" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.

First, we need to parameterize a part-circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin. This curve can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+9{sin}^{2}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+9{sin}^{2}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-9\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+27{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =9\operatorname{cos}⁡t(3{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }9\operatorname{cos}⁡t(3{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & =9{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t(3{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & =9{[{sin}^{3}⁡t-\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡t}{2}]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =9[0-(1-\frac{1}{2})] \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-17a6c1da-e7e7-5509-a937-e43376741415" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-a60002fd-79c9-55af-8350-d15ad8aa640e" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i-x\,j \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-{sin}^{2}⁡t-{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =-({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-1)\,dt \\  & ={-t|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-2\pi \end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186180015 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-84019ffa-a424-5feb-9be8-03a303ad719a" :answer-field/id #uuid "84019ffa-a424-5feb-9be8-03a303ad719a"] $$

First, we need to parameterize a circle of radius $4$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+y\,j \\  & =-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,dt \\  & =-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t){|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-8+8 \\  & =0\end{aligned}

:question/problem "Evaluate $\displaystyle \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf F(x, y) = y\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}$ and $C$ is a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction." :question/worked-solution "The notation $\displaystyle\oint$ is used to remind us that we're dealing with a line integral over a *closed* curve.

We will use the formula

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} + \sin{t}\,\mathbf{j},
\qquad 0 \leq t \lt 2\pi.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = \cos{t}, \qquad
y = \sin{t}.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,j=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =-(1-{cos}^{2}⁡t)+{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡t-1 \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048655} {:db/id 17592186049512} {:db/id 17592186050616} {:db/id 17592186180015 :question/id #uuid "2a8909b1-1a48-5c56-ac06-8b954196fc3e" :question/math-academy-id "q-124936" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179735 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5d7c30c2-5d42-5648-ae49-5a0c7ec43233" :knowledge-point/title "Line Integrals Over Circles and Ellipses"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a3c563c9-8c9b-55da-b8c2-070042347609" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "- π" :db/id 17592186177760} {:answer/id #uuid "0dde43ea-dd20-502b-9156-72d9581da6f2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186177761} {:answer/id #uuid "19255a63-77b4-5533-9b49-2a20815502be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "π" :db/id 17592186177762} {:answer/id #uuid "4a62c57f-bb46-535a-bd54-25ff210b61f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186177763} {:answer/id #uuid "6480e3a7-53e0-513b-b505-7959ab4767ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2π" :db/id 17592186177764}] :answer-field/id #uuid "d6a48da5-21ec-5631-9f71-f7840fbba2c2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186177759}] :question/problem "Evaluate $∮_(C)F(r) \cdot dr$, where $F(x, y) = yi - $$
y^3 = x-5
\qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad
x = y^3 + 5.
$$

So, we can parametrize the curve using

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =({t}^{3}+5)\,i+t\,j,\,0\le t\le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
x = t^3+5, \qquad
y = t.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,j \\  & =t\,i+({t}^{3}+5)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+5)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =3{t}^{2}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i+({t}^{3}+5)\,j)\cdot (3{t}^{2}\,i+j) \\  & =t\cdot 3{t}^{2}+({t}^{3}+5)\cdot 1 \\  & =3{t}^{3}+{t}^{3}+5 \\  & =4{t}^{3}+5.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{t}^{3}+5\,dt \\  & ={[{t}^{4}+5t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =1+5-0 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048645} {:db/id 17592186049633} {:db/id 17592186180012 :question/id #uuid "d4e0663c-1824-56f9-b923-60eb7cd3a338" :question/math-academy-id "q-124703" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179736 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f6eddefb-d4b9-5e5b-9278-94de0d8dbff6" :knowledge-point/title "Line Integrals Over Cartesian Curves"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c6434469-1749-5df8-9000-f01893b94638" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\displaystyle \int_{1}^{2}\sin t + 4t\sin (t^{2})dt" :db/id 17592186177742} {:answer/id #uuid "f39fe168-22ec-5e69-aafa-66a8710a1fd9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\displaystyle \int_{1}^{2}\sin t + 4t\sin (t^{2} - 1)dt" :db/id 17592186177743} {:answer/id #uuid "08e97c23-852d-5a73-b52f-061e3a0c40e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\displaystyle \int_{1}^{2}\cos t + 4t\sin (2t^{2} - 1)dt" :db/id 17592186177744} {:answer/id #uuid "28257dfc-7abd-5d10-8977-76f400b99f65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1}\cos t + 4t\sin (2t^{2} - 1)dt" :db/id 17592186177745} {:answer/id #uuid "33b189d2-9b33-585b-8051-e116d98891cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1}\sin t + 4t\cos (t^{2})dt" :db/id 17592186177746}] :answer-field/id #uuid "281b8c1b-0aa5-57dc-b60a-9cd72b4bdf28" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186177741}] :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to the integral $\displaystyle \int_(C)F \cdot dr$, where $F(x, y) = \cos xi + \sin yj$ and $C$ is the curve $y = 2x^{2} - 1$ traversed from the point $A(1, 1)$ to the point $B(2, 7)$?

:question/problem "Evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf F(x, y) =(1-y)^2\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}$ and $C$ is the line segment traversed from the point $A(0, 2)$ to the point $B(1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the line segment.
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are 
$\mathbf{a} = 2\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{i}.$
So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =2j+t[i-2j] \\  & =t\,i+(2-2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t$ varies from $t=0$ (at the point $A$) to $t = 1$ (at the point $B$).
Thus, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = t, \qquad
	y = 2-2t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(1-y)^{2}\,i+x\,j \\  & =(1-(2-2t))^{2}\,i+t\,j \\  & =(2t-1)^{2}\,i+t\,j \\  & =(4{t}^{2}-4t+1)\,i+t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-2t)j \\  & =i-2j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((4{t}^{2}-4t+1)\,i+t\,j)\cdot (i-2j) \\  & =(4{t}^{2}-4t+1)\cdot (1)+(t)\cdot (-2) \\  & =4{t}^{2}-6t+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{t}^{2}-6t+1\,dt \\  & =(\frac{4}{3}{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}+t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{4}{3}-3+1)-0 \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048512} {:db/id 17592186049853} {:db/id 17592186180010 :question/id #uuid "88b31475-15e6-5485-a3fc-dfd5113d0f64" :question/math-academy-id "q-124701"} {:db/id 17592186180011 $$

\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r .
$$

This integral represents the total work done by $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle from an initial point $A$ to a terminal point $B$ along the curve.

If the curve can be parameterized by the function $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ then we can calculate the line integral using the following formula:

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r= \int_a^b \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t)\,\textrm dt
$$

Often, the trickiest part is finding a parameterization for $C.$ In this lesson, we'll consider several different cases" :tutorial/id #uuid "ec010a30-571c-5ad5-b30a-c18ffdd997e1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5823 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7b85eebf-c70c-58a0-9476-5bcb73727ad3" :step/math-academy-id 35690 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180491}} {:db/id 17592186180718 :tutorial/content "The line integral of a vector-valued function $\mathbf F$ along a piecewise smooth curve $C$ is denoted

Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.
Students then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.
Applications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.
The course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
Students next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.
Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.
The course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.
Laplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.
The course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics. Students analyze the accuracy and stability of numerical schemes used in computational physics and study multivariate probability distributions and the central limit theorem, which appear in remind us that we're dealing with a line integral over a *closed* curve.

We will use the formula

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,\textrm{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize a circle of radius $1$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} + \sin{t}\,\mathbf{j},
\qquad 0 \leq t \lt 2\pi.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = \cos{t}, \qquad
